claim: TRP channels are a large and diverse family of tetrameric cation-selective channels.
source: Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels are a large and diverse family of tetrameric cation-selective channels that are activated by many different types of stimuli, including noxious heat or cold, organic ligands such as vanilloids or cooling agents, or intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TRP channels, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: TRP channels are activated by many different types of stimuli, including noxious heat or cold, organic ligands such as vanilloids or cooling agents, or intracellular Ca2+.
source: Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels are a large and diverse family of tetrameric cation-selective channels that are activated by many different types of stimuli, including noxious heat or cold, organic ligands such as vanilloids or cooling agents, or intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TRP channel activation mechanisms.

claim: Structures available for all subtypes of TRP channels reveal that the transmembrane domains are closely related despite their unique sensitivity to activating stimuli.
source: Structures available for all subtypes of TRP channels reveal that the transmembrane domains are closely related despite their unique sensitivity to activating stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of TRP channels from the literature.

claim: A subset of TRPM channels, including TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5, contain pockets very similar to the cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM8.

evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by structural alignment data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The cooling agent icilin modulates activation of mouse TRPM4 to intracellular Ca2+.
source: We then show how the cooling agent icilin modulates activation of mouse TRPM4 to intracellular Ca2+, enhancing the sensitivity of the channel to Ca2+ and diminishing outward-rectification to promote opening at negative voltages.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Icilin enhances the sensitivity of TRPM4 to Ca2+.
source: We then show how the cooling agent icilin modulates activation of mouse TRPM4 to intracellular Ca2+, enhancing the sensitivity of the channel to Ca2+ and diminishing outward-rectification to promote opening at negative voltages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 3.

claim: Icilin diminishes outward-rectification of TRPM4 to promote opening at negative voltages.

claim: Mutations known to promote or diminish activation of TRPM8 by cooling agents similarly alter activation of TRPM4 by icilin.
source: Mutations known to promote or diminish activation of TRPM8 by cooling agents similarly alter activation of TRPM4 by icilin, suggesting that icilin binds to the cooling agent binding pocket to promote opening of the channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figures 5-8.

claim: Icilin binds to the cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM4 to promote opening of the channel.
source: Mutations known to promote or diminish activation of TRPM8 by cooling agents similarly alter activation of TRPM4 by icilin, suggesting that icilin binds to the cooling agent binding pocket to promote opening of the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data and structural conservation.

claim: TRPM4 and TRPM8 channels share related ligand binding pockets that are allosterically coupled to opening of the pore.
source: These findings demonstrate that TRPM4 and TRPM8 channels share related ligand binding pockets that are allosterically coupled to opening of the pore.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and structural analysis.

claim: A Drosophila trp mutant was discovered to exhibit a transient receptor potential in electroretinogram recordings.
source: The founding member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel family was cloned two decades after a Drosophila trp mutant was discovered to exhibit a transient receptor potential in electroretinogram recordings (Cosens and Manning, 1969; Montell and Rubin, 1989; Wong et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical research.

source: All TRP channels are tetrameric cation channels that contain six transmembrane (TM) segments (S1–S6) per subunit (Figure 1), similar to voltage-activated K+ channels (Cao, 2020; Huffer et al., 2020).

claim: TRPV1 functions as a detector of noxious heat in mammals.
source: Two of the most extensively studied TRP channels are TRPV1 and TRPM8, which in mammals function as detectors of noxious heat (Caterina et al., 1997; Tominaga et al., 1998; Caterina et al., 2000) and noxious cold (McKemy et al., 2002; Peier et al., 2002; Bautista et al., 2007; Dhaka et al., 2007), respectively.

source: Vanilloids and cooling agents were originally proposed to bind to similar regions of TRPV1 and TRPM8 because mutations affecting channel activation by these compounds could be found in similar TM regions (Chuang et al., 2004).

claim: Structures solved using cryo-EM have revealed that vanilloids bind to a membrane-facing pocket positioned at the interface between the pore domain formed by S5–S6 and the peripheral S1–S4 domains.
source: However, structures solved using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have since revealed that vanilloids bind to a membrane-facing pocket positioned at the interface between the pore domain formed by S5–S6 and the peripheral S1–S4 domains (Cao et al., 2013b; Liao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021), whereas cooling agents bind within a pocket formed entirely by the S1–S4 helices that opens to the cytoplasm (Yin et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin and Lee, 2020; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structures and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Cooling agents bind within a pocket formed entirely by the S1–S4 helices that opens to the cytoplasm.
source: However, structures solved using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have since revealed that vanilloids bind to a membrane-facing pocket positioned at the interface between the pore domain formed by S5–S6 and the peripheral S1–S4 domains (Cao et al., 2013b; Liao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021), whereas cooling agents bind within a pocket formed entirely by the S1–S4 helices that opens to the cytoplasm (Yin et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin and Lee, 2020; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structures and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The vanilloid binding pocket in TRPV1 can be occupied by vanilloid agonists and antagonists.
source: The vanilloid binding pocket in TRPV1 can be occupied by vanilloid agonists and antagonists (Cao et al., 2013b; Liao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Kwon et al., 2022; Neuberger et al., 2023), in addition to membrane lipids that have been proposed to stabilize a closed state of the channel (Cao et al., 2013a; Gao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021; Arnold et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Membrane lipids have been proposed to stabilize a closed state of TRPV1 by occupying the vanilloid binding pocket.
source: The vanilloid binding pocket in TRPV1 can be occupied by vanilloid agonists and antagonists (Cao et al., 2013b; Liao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Kwon et al., 2022; Neuberger et al., 2023), in addition to membrane lipids that have been proposed to stabilize a closed state of the channel (Cao et al., 2013a; Gao et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021; Arnold et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Cryo-EM maps for all five available TRPM8 structures with icilin bound show a large non-protein density consistent with icilin nestled within the S1–S4 domain.
source: Cryo-EM maps for all five available TRPM8 structures with the cooling agent icilin bound (6nr3, 7wrc, 7wrd, 7wre, and 7wrf) show a large non-protein density consistent with icilin nestled within the S1–S4 domain (Yin et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin and Lee, 2020; Zhao et al., 2022; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structures and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM8 is lined by residues where mutations are known to modulate sensitivity to icilin and/or menthol.
source: This cooling agent binding pocket is lined by residues where mutations are known to modulate sensitivity to icilin and/or the cooling agent menthol (Chuang et al., 2004; Bandell et al., 2006; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin and Lee, 2020; Zhao et al., 2022), supporting the assignment of this density to icilin during model building (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutagenesis studies and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Other TRPM8 ligands have been observed in the cooling agent binding pocket, including cooling agents WS-12 and C3 and antagonists AMTB, TC-I 2014, and AMG2850.
source: Other TRPM8 ligands have also been observed in this pocket, including cooling agents WS-12 (6nr2) and C3 (8e4l, 8e4m, 9b6h) and the antagonists AMTB (6o6r, 9b6g), TC-I 2014 (6o72, 9b6e, 9b6h, 9b6i), and AMG2850 (9b6f) (Diver et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin and Lee, 2020; Yin et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structures.

claim: Other TRP channel structures from the Canonical and Vanilloid subfamilies show small molecule ligands bound to a similar location within the S1–S4 domain.
source: Interestingly, other TRP channel structures from the Canonical and Vanilloid subfamilies also show small molecule ligands bound to a similar location within the S1–S4 domain (7b0s, 7b05, 7wdb, 7d4p, 6uza, 7dxg, 6dvy, 6dvz, 7ras, 7rau, 6pbe, 6d7o, 6d7q, 6d7t, 6d7v, 6d7x) (Singh et al., 2018a, Singh et al., 2018b; Hughes et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2020; Vinayagam et al., 2020; Neuberger et al., 2021; Song et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2022), raising the possibility that this pocket may be a hot spot for ligand modulation across the TRP channel family.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: The S1–S4 ligand binding pocket may be a hot spot for ligand modulation across the TRP channel family.
source: Interestingly, other TRP channel structures from the Canonical and Vanilloid subfamilies also show small molecule ligands bound to a similar location within the S1–S4 domain (7b0s, 7b05, 7wdb, 7d4p, 6uza, 7dxg, 6dvy, 6dvz, 7ras, 7rau, 6pbe, 6d7o, 6d7q, 6d7t, 6d7v, 6d7x) (Singh et al., 2018a, Singh et al., 2018b; Hughes et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2020; Vinayagam et al., 2020; Neuberger et al., 2021; Song et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2022), raising the possibility that this pocket may be a hot spot for ligand modulation across the TRP channel family.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural observations.

claim: The cytoplasmic entrance to the cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM8 contains a binding site for a Ca2+ ion.
source: The cytoplasmic entrance to the cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM8 also contains a binding site for a Ca2+ ion (6nr3, 7wrb, 7wrc, 7wrd, 7wre, 7wrf, 8e4l, 8e4m, 6o77, 9b6i, 9b6j, 9b6k) (Figure 1; Diver et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structures and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Ca2+ alone has not been described to modulate TRPM8 activity.
source: While Ca2+ alone has not been described to modulate TRPM8 activity, it is an essential cofactor for activation of TRPM8 by icilin (Chuang et al., 2004), and several residues, including E782 in S2 and D802 in S3 of TRPM8 from Ficedula albicollis (faTRPM8) and mouse (mTRPM8), are located within 4 Å of both the Ca2+ ion and the icilin molecule (Yin et al., 2019a; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ca2+ is an essential cofactor for activation of TRPM8 by icilin.
source: While Ca2+ alone has not been described to modulate TRPM8 activity, it is an essential cofactor for activation of TRPM8 by icilin (Chuang et al., 2004), and several residues, including E782 in S2 and D802 in S3 of TRPM8 from Ficedula albicollis (faTRPM8) and mouse (mTRPM8), are located within 4 Å of both the Ca2+ ion and the icilin molecule (Yin et al., 2019a; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: E782 in S2 and D802 in S3 of TRPM8 are located within 4 Å of both the Ca2+ ion and the icilin molecule.
source: While Ca2+ alone has not been described to modulate TRPM8 activity, it is an essential cofactor for activation of TRPM8 by icilin (Chuang et al., 2004), and several residues, including E782 in S2 and D802 in S3 of TRPM8 from Ficedula albicollis (faTRPM8) and mouse (mTRPM8), are located within 4 Å of both the Ca2+ ion and the icilin molecule (Yin et al., 2019a; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Mutations in N799 and D802 in S3 of TRPM8 have been implicated in selective loss of icilin sensitivity.
source: Mutations in N799 and D802 in S3 of TRPM8 from rats (rTRPM8) and humans (hTRPM8) have been implicated in selective loss of icilin sensitivity (Chuang et al., 2004; Winking et al., 2012; Kühn et al., 2013; Beccari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutagenesis studies.

claim: N799 does not contact the icilin molecule directly.
source: Because N799 does not contact the icilin molecule directly, it presumably perturbs icilin sensitivity by disrupting binding of the obligate cofactor, Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: N799 presumably perturbs icilin sensitivity by disrupting binding of the obligate cofactor, Ca2+.
source: Because N799 does not contact the icilin molecule directly, it presumably perturbs icilin sensitivity by disrupting binding of the obligate cofactor, Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and mutagenesis data.

source: Interestingly, the equivalent Ca2+-binding site has been observed in several other TRPM channel structures (6bqv, 6co7, 6d73, 6drj, 6nr3, 6o77, 6pkx, 6pus, 6puu, 7mbq, 7mbs, 7mbu, 7mbv, 7wrb, 7wrc, 7wrd, 7wre, 7wrf) (Autzen et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018b, Diver et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin et al., 2019b; Ruan et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022), including TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5, for which intracellular Ca2+ is the key physiological agonist, and where mutations to the Ca2+-coordinating residues have been shown to alter channel activation by intracellular Ca2+ (Guo et al., 2017; Autzen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018b, Yamaguchi et al., 2019).

source: Interestingly, the equivalent Ca2+-binding site has been observed in several other TRPM channel structures (6bqv, 6co7, 6d73, 6drj, 6nr3, 6o77, 6pkx, 6pus, 6puu, 7mbq, 7mbs, 7mbu, 7mbv, 7wrb, 7wrc, 7wrd, 7wre, 7wrf) (Autzen et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018b, Diver et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin et al., 2019b; Ruan et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022), including TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5, for which intracellular Ca2+ is the key physiological agonist, and where mutations to the Ca2+-coordinating residues have been shown to alter channel activation by intracellular Ca2+ (Guo et al., 2017; Autzen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018b, Yamaguchi et al., 2019).

evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The presence of the ion-binding pocket within the S1–S4 domains across the TRP channel family indicates that it is a key regulatory location.
source: As in the cooling agent binding pocket, the presence of this ion-binding pocket within the S1–S4 domains across the TRP channel family indicates that it is another key regulatory location.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the ion-binding site across TRP channels.

claim: TRPV2 and TRPV3 are insensitive to the TRPV1-specific high-affinity vanilloid agonist Resiniferatoxin (RTx).
source: For example, TRPV2 and TRPV3 are insensitive to the TRPV1-specific high-affinity vanilloid agonist Resiniferatoxin (RTx), but sensitivity to this vanilloid can be readily engineered into both TRPV channels by mutating only a few key residues within the vanilloid binding site (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019), revealing that the mechanisms responsible for coupling occupancy of the vanilloid site to channel opening are conserved in these three TRPV channels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sensitivity to RTx can be readily engineered into TRPV2 and TRPV3 by mutating only a few key residues within the vanilloid binding site.

claim: The icilin binding pocket was defined to include residues located near the icilin molecules in the available icilin-bound TRPM8 structures.
source: We defined the icilin binding pocket to include residues located near the icilin molecules in the available icilin-bound TRPM8 structures.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The electron densities attributed to icilin lack sufficient definition to fit the asymmetric functional groups in all but one of the five icilin-bound structures.
source: Unfortunately, the electron densities attributed to icilin lack sufficient definition to fit these asymmetric functional groups in all but one of the five icilin-bound structures, even though the S1–S4 helices have relatively high local resolution in these structures.
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: The structure with the most asymmetric icilin density (7wrd) is not the highest resolution structure (7wre).
source: Interestingly, the structure with the most asymmetric icilin density (7wrd, with 2.98 Å overall nominal resolution) is not the highest resolution structure (7wre, with 2.52 Å overall nominal resolution).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: Both icilin binding poses in structures 7wrd and 7wre are similarly plausible.
source: Previous comparison of these two binding poses has indicated that both poses are similarly plausible (Palchevskyi et al., 2023), although the energy minimization performed in this study was conducted in the absence of the obligate cofactor, Ca2+, which may be important for stabilizing icilin binding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior computational analysis.

claim: The icilin binding pocket includes residues within 4 Å of the icilin molecule in either pose (6nr3 or 7wre).
source: We chose to use the most inclusive definition of binding pocket lining residues, counting any residue that was within 4 Å of the icilin molecule in either pose (6nr3 or 7wre), which also included all interacting residues identified by PoseFilter (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Ca2+-coordinating residues were included in the binding pocket definition because Ca2+ is an essential cofactor.
source: In addition, we included the Ca2+-coordinating residues in the binding pocket because Ca2+ is an essential cofactor and mutations in Ca2+-coordinating residues have been described to specifically disrupt icilin sensitivity in TRPM8 (Chuang et al., 2004; Winking et al., 2012; Kühn et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the methodology and is supported by citations.

claim: The cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM8 shows high conservation in TRPM2 (78% identical), TRPM4 (89% identical) and TRPM5 (94% identical).
source: Comparing other Melastatin subfamily channels to TRPM8 revealed unexpectedly high conservation in the residues lining the cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM2 (78% identical), TRPM4 (89% identical) and TRPM5 (94% identical) (Figure 2), channels that have not previously been reported to be sensitive to icilin.
evidence: This is a finding from structural alignment analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5 have not previously been reported to be sensitive to icilin.
source: Comparing other Melastatin subfamily channels to TRPM8 revealed unexpectedly high conservation in the residues lining the cooling agent binding pocket in TRPM2 (78% identical), TRPM4 (89% identical) and TRPM5 (94% identical) (Figure 2), channels that have not previously been reported to be sensitive to icilin.

claim: Mutations of residues in the cooling agent binding pocket of TRPM8 are known to functionally influence cooling agent sensitivity.
source: Mutations of residues in the structurally identified cooling agent binding pocket located within the S1–S4 domain of rTRPM8, including those corresponding to Y745 in S1, Q785 in S2, N799 and D802 in S3, R842 and H845 in S4, and Y1005 in the TRP box, are known to functionally influence cooling agent sensitivity in mTRPM8, rTRPM8, hTRPM8, Parus major TRPM8 (pmTRPM8) or faTRPM8 (Chuang et al., 2004; Bandell et al., 2006; Voets et al., 2007; Malkia et al., 2009; Winking et al., 2012; Kühn et al., 2013; Beccari et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2018; Diver et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin and Lee, 2020; Plaza-Cayón et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022).

claim: TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5 show structural similarity to TRPM8 in the shape of the cooling agent binding pocket and orientation of the equivalent residues.
source: These important residues (Figure 2A; red asterisks), along with other residues located within 4 Å of icilin or Ca2+ in TRPM8 (Figure 2A; blue highlighting), are highly conserved between TRPM8 and TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5. These channels also show structural similarity in the shape of the pocket and orientation of the equivalent residues (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: G805 in rTRPM8 is conserved in mammalian TRPM8 channels that are sensitive to icilin, but is substituted by an Ala in avian TRPM8 channels that are insensitive to icilin.
source: The one notable and important difference near the cooling agent binding pocket between TRPM8, TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5 is at the position corresponding to G805 in rTRPM8, a position that is conserved in mammalian TRPM8 channels that are sensitive to icilin, but is substituted by an Ala in avian TRPM8 channels that are insensitive to icilin (Chuang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5 might be insensitive to icilin but could be rendered sensitive to icilin by substituting a Gly at the position corresponding to G805 in TRPM8.
source: Because this critical position in TRPM8 is an Ala in most other TRPM channels (Figure 2), we predicted that TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM5 might be insensitive to icilin but could be rendered sensitive to icilin by substituting a Gly, similar to the icilin-sensitizing mutants engineered into avian TRPM8 channels (Chuang et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a prediction based on structural analysis and prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: TRPM3 and TRPM7 show less conservation in the icilin- and Ca2+-adjacent residues (44% identity in both cases) compared to TRPM8.
source: In the case of TRPM3 and TRPM7, in addition to lacking the critical Gly residue, there is less conservation in the icilin- and Ca2+-adjacent residues (44% identity in both cases) (Figure 2), suggesting that these channels may not be sensitive to icilin.
evidence: This is a finding from structural alignment analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: TRPM3 and TRPM7 may not be sensitive to icilin.
source: In the case of TRPM3 and TRPM7, in addition to lacking the critical Gly residue, there is less conservation in the icilin- and Ca2+-adjacent residues (44% identity in both cases) (Figure 2), suggesting that these channels may not be sensitive to icilin.
evidence: This is a prediction based on structural analysis.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TRPM4 is relatively impermeable to Ca2+.

evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: mTRPM4 exhibits an outwardly rectifying current–voltage (I–V) relation in the presence of Ca2+.

claim: The Ca2+ sensitivity measured after the first Ca2+ application is similar to previously reported EC50 values for TRPM4 in inside-out patches that have not been supplemented with PIP2.
